claim: Several risk factors for pediatric asthma can be ascertained in the perinatal period, including maternal characteristics (e.g., maternal atopy, maternal body mass index [BMI], race/ethnicity), demographics (e.g., newborn sex), and birth characteristics (e.g., birthweight, gestational age at birth, mode of delivery).
source: Several risk factors for pediatric asthma can be ascertained in the perinatal period. These risk factors include maternal characteristics (e.g., maternal atopy, maternal body mass index [BMI], race/ethnicity), demographics (e.g., newborn sex), and birth characteristics (e.g., birthweight, gestational age at birth, mode of delivery) (Bisgaard and Bønnelykke, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bisgaard and Bønnelykke, 2010.

claim: Meta-analyses have provided strong evidence for associations between maternal atopy, maternal BMI, race/ethnicity, newborn sex, birthweight, gestational age at birth, mode of delivery and risk for pediatric asthma.
source: Meta-analyses have provided strong evidence for associations between the variables stated above and risk for pediatric asthma (Jaakkola et al., 2006; Mu et al., 2014; Thavagnanam et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple meta-analyses (Jaakkola et al., 2006; Mu et al., 2014; Thavagnanam et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2014).

claim: Many perinatal risk factors for pediatric asthma co-occur (e.g., low birthweight and preterm birth).
source: Many of these risk factors co-occur (e.g., low birthweight and preterm birth), and it has yet to be discerned whether their imparted risk is mediated through similar biologic processes.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about co-occurrence of risk factors.

claim: Meta-analyses assessing peripheral blood leukocytes of school-aged children have identified differentially methylated regions proximal, or within, genes specifically transcribed in eosinophils as a common signature in pediatric asthma.
source: Meta-analyses assessing peripheral blood leukocytes of school-aged children have identified differentially methylated regions proximal, or within, genes specifically transcribed in eosinophils as a common signature in pediatric asthma (Xu et al., 2018; Reese et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2018 and Reese et al., 2019.

claim: Differential methylation in eosinophil-associated genes is consistent with observations of enhanced T2 inflammatory responses in children with asthma.
source: These findings are consistent with observations of enhanced T2 inflammatory responses in children with asthma (Wenzel, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wenzel, 2012.

claim: When assessing cord blood mononuclear cell (CBMC) samples, differential methylation did not extend to eosinophil-associated and other classically T2-associated loci.
source: However, when assessing cord blood mononuclear cell (CBMC) samples, differential methylation did not extend to these and other classically T2-associated loci (Reese et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Reese et al., 2019.

claim: Some individuals are predisposed at birth to generating T2 responses ex vivo to common asthma triggers or having detectable IgE concentrations in cord blood.
source: Interestingly, some individuals are predisposed at birth to generating T2 responses ex vivo to common asthma triggers (e.g. aeroallergens) or having detectable IgE concentrations in cord blood but neither has been shown to predict asthma later in life (Schaub et al., 2005; Turturice et al., 2017a; Shah et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schaub et al., 2005; Turturice et al., 2017a; Shah et al., 2011.

claim: Neither T2 responses ex vivo to common asthma triggers nor detectable IgE concentrations in cord blood have been shown to predict asthma later in life.
source: Interestingly, some individuals are predisposed at birth to generating T2 responses ex vivo to common asthma triggers (e.g. aeroallergens) or having detectable IgE concentrations in cord blood but neither has been shown to predict asthma later in life (Schaub et al., 2005; Turturice et al., 2017a; Shah et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schaub et al., 2005; Turturice et al., 2017a; Shah et al., 2011.

claim: Efforts aimed at modulating immunity in utero and through early life (e.g. vitamin D, probiotics) have failed to demonstrate benefit in the prevention of asthma.
source: Additionally, efforts aimed at modulating immunity in utero and through early life (e.g. vitamin D, probiotics) have failed to demonstrate benefit in the prevention of asthma (Litonjua et al., 2020; Azad et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Litonjua et al., 2020 and Azad et al., 2013.

claim: Throughout the majority of gestation, fetal hematopoiesis generates mainly lymphoid and erythroid lineages.
source: Throughout the majority of gestation, fetal hematopoiesis generates mainly lymphoid and erythroid lineages.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about fetal hematopoiesis.

claim: The bone marrow capacity to produce all cell lineages increases toward term gestation, with the ability to produce myeloid lineages being most pronounced in later gestational ages.
source: While the bone marrow capacity to produce all cell lineages increases toward term gestation, the ability to produce myeloid lineages is most pronounced in later gestational ages (Forestier et al., 1991; Glasser et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Forestier et al., 1991 and Glasser et al., 2015.

claim: CXCL8-producing T cells and myeloid-derived suppressor cells are highly abundant in cord blood and are rapidly depleted over the first week.
source: Further highlighting the unique immunology of the perinatal time period, there are cell populations (e.g. CXCL8-producing T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells) that are highly abundant in cord blood that are rapidly depleted over the first week (Gibbons et al., 2014; Olin et al., 2018; Rieber et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gibbons et al., 2014; Olin et al., 2018; Rieber et al., 2013.

claim: In utero factors, such as preterm birth and gestational hypertension, can impact perinatal hematopoiesis and impair neutrophil abundance and function at birth.
source: Importantly, in utero factors, such as preterm birth and gestational hypertension, can impact perinatal hematopoiesis. These events can impair neutrophil abundance and function at birth but return to adult levels within days of birth similar to that of those who did not have such an exposure (Glasser et al., 2015; Olin et al., 2018; Schmutz et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Glasser et al., 2015; Olin et al., 2018; Schmutz et al., 2008.

claim: Neutrophil abundance and function impaired by in utero factors return to adult levels within days of birth.
source: These events can impair neutrophil abundance and function at birth but return to adult levels within days of birth similar to that of those who did not have such an exposure (Glasser et al., 2015; Olin et al., 2018; Schmutz et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Glasser et al., 2015; Olin et al., 2018; Schmutz et al., 2008.

claim: The study identified 354 datasets from the original search of NCBI's Gene Expression Omnibus for CBMC microarray datasets.
source: We identified 354 datasets from our original search, of which 17 datasets contained relevant metadata.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the study's search process.

claim: Of the 354 datasets identified, 17 datasets contained relevant metadata regarding demographics and birth characteristics that are risk factors for pediatric asthma.
source: We identified 354 datasets from our original search, of which 17 datasets contained relevant metadata.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the study's search process.

claim: Newborn sex, gestational age at birth, birthweight, and maternal pre-pregnancy BMI were reported at 69.96%, 51.59%, 30.27%, and 19.32% of samples, respectively.
source: Of the 17 studies, the most common maternal and neonatal characteristics reported were newborn sex, gestational age at birth, birthweight, and maternal pre-pregnancy BMI (PP BMI) at 69.96%, 51.59%, 30.27%, and 19.32% of samples, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the study's analysis of available datasets.

claim: A total of 605 unique transcriptomes were included in the meta-analysis.
source: Datasets and the corresponding analysis are reported; a total of 605 unique transcriptomes were included (Table 1; Bukowski et al., 2017; Edlow et al., 2016; Kallionpää et al., 2014; Mason et al., 2010; Rager et al., 2014; Smith et al., 2014; Stünkel et al., 2012; Turan et al., 2012; Votavova et al., 2011; Votavova et al., 2012; Winckelmans et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the study's meta-analysis.

claim: Differential expression (false discovery rate [FDR] < 1%) was observed in 122 genes when comparing fetal sex.
source: Differential expression (false discovery rate [FDR] < 1%) was observed in 122, 34, 4, and 12 genes when comparing fetal sex, gestational age, birthweight, and maternal pre-pregnancy BMI, respectively (Supplementary file 1–4).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the study's univariate random-effects models.

claim: Differential expression (false discovery rate [FDR] < 1%) was observed in 34 genes when comparing gestational age.
source: Differential expression (false discovery rate [FDR] < 1%) was observed in 122, 34, 4, and 12 genes when comparing fetal sex, gestational age, birthweight, and maternal pre-pregnancy BMI, respectively (Supplementary file 1–4).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the study's univariate random-effects models.

claim: Differential expression (false discovery rate [FDR] < 1%) was observed in 4 genes when comparing birthweight.
source: Differential expression (false discovery rate [FDR] < 1%) was observed in 122, 34, 4, and 12 genes when comparing fetal sex, gestational age, birthweight, and maternal pre-pregnancy BMI, respectively (Supplementary file 1–4).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the study's univariate random-effects models.

claim: Differential expression (false discovery rate [FDR] < 1%) was observed in 12 genes when comparing maternal pre-pregnancy BMI.
source: Differential expression (false discovery rate [FDR] < 1%) was observed in 122, 34, 4, and 12 genes when comparing fetal sex, gestational age, birthweight, and maternal pre-pregnancy BMI, respectively (Supplementary file 1–4).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the study's univariate random-effects models.

claim: Several genes located on X (KDM5C, SMC1A, TXLNG, and KDM6A) and Y (KDM5D and EIF1AY) chromosomes exhibited the largest effect sizes and most significant differences in sex-associated transcriptional changes.
source: With regards to sex-associated transcriptional changes, although there was no X or Y chromosome-wide gene enrichment, several genes located on X (KDM5C, SMC1A, TXLNG, and KDM6A) and Y (KDM5D and EIF1AY) chromosomes exhibited the largest effect sizes and most significant differences.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the study's sex-associated transcriptional analysis.

claim: HBE1, a hemoglobin subunit associated with fetal erythropoiesis, was significantly associated with preterm gestational ages.
source: In addition to expected sex-associated transcriptional changes, HBE1, a hemoglobin subunit associated with fetal erythropoiesis, was significantly associated with preterm gestational ages.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the study's gestational age analysis.

claim: A significant association was observed between differentially methylated genes and the effect size in the gestational age analysis, such that genes whose methylation increased with gestational age showed on average decreased expression with gestational age.
source: A significant association was observed between differentially methylated genes and the effect size in our gestational age analysis, such that genes whose methylation increased with gestational age as reported by Bohlin et al., 2016 showed on average decreased expression with gestational age in our meta-analysis.
evidence: The claim is based on data comparing the study's results with previously published results from Bohlin et al., 2016, as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: 18 GO terms were significantly enriched (FDR < 1%) with regards to low-risk profiles.
source: GO terms were assessed for enrichment; 18 and 19 GO terms were significantly enriched (FDR < 1%) with regards to low- and high-risk profiles, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on data from gene set enrichment analysis, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 19 GO terms were significantly enriched (FDR < 1%) with regards to high-risk profiles.
source: GO terms were assessed for enrichment; 18 and 19 GO terms were significantly enriched (FDR < 1%) with regards to low- and high-risk profiles, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on data from gene set enrichment analysis, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Genes associated with lower risk exhibited increased representation in GO terms involving innate immune signaling and defense.
source: Genes associated with lower risk exhibited increased representation in GO terms involving innate immune signaling and defense, whereas high-risk genes were enriched in pathways involving translation and RNA metabolic processes.
evidence: The claim is based on data from gene set enrichment analysis, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: High-risk genes were enriched in pathways involving translation and RNA metabolic processes.
source: Genes associated with lower risk exhibited increased representation in GO terms involving innate immune signaling and defense, whereas high-risk genes were enriched in pathways involving translation and RNA metabolic processes.
evidence: The claim is based on data from gene set enrichment analysis, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A generalized increase in expression of low-risk genes in myeloid cells and high-risk genes in lymphoid cells was observed.
source: We observed a generalized increase in expression of low-risk genes in myeloid cells and high-risk genes in lymphoid cells.
evidence: The claim is based on data from analysis using the Human Protein Atlas, as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The pattern of expression of low-risk genes in myeloid cells and high-risk genes in lymphoid cells was most pronounced in neutrophils.
source: This pattern of expression was most pronounced in neutrophils (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on data from analysis using the Human Protein Atlas, as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lower risk individuals have increased populations of myeloid cells in their CBMCs.
source: These results suggest that lower risk individuals have increased populations of myeloid cells in their CBMCs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed pattern of gene expression in different cell types.

claim: The highest correlations with the pooled z-score were the z-scores from the meta-analyses assessing gestational age at birth, newborn sex, and birthweight.
source: The highest correlations with the pooled z-score were the z-scores from the meta-analyses assessing gestational age at birth, newborn sex, and birthweight.
evidence: The claim is based on data from correlation analysis, as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The pooled z-score amalgamates information across all of the analyses, with the most influence arising from gestational age at birth, newborn sex, and birthweight.
source: Together, this demonstrates that the pooled z-score does, indeed, amalgamate information across all of the analyses, with the most influence arising from gestational age at birth, newborn sex, and birthweight.
evidence: The claim is based on data from correlation analysis.

claim: Fifty-one genes had a replication score (RS) greater than 3.
source: Fifty-one genes, 0.4% of all genes, tested had a RS greater than 3 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the validation analysis comparing the meta-analysis with the UIH cohort, as shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Genes with RS greater than 3 corresponded well with the results of pooled z-score for gestational age at birth, newborn sex and birthweight, but showed limited correlation to maternal PP BMI.
source: These identified genes corresponded well with the results of pooled z-score for gestational age at birth, newborn sex and birthweight, but showed limited correlation to maternal PP BMI.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the validation analysis.

claim: Genes with RS greater than 3 had median p-values of 0.02, 0.01, 0.11, and 0.58 in the gestational age at birth, newborn sex, birthweight, and maternal PP BMI meta-analyses, respectively.
source: They had median p-values of 0.02, 0.01, 0.11, and 0.58 in the gestational age at birth, newborn sex, birthweight, and maternal PP BMI meta-analyses, and median p-value of 0.02 in the UIH cohort.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the validation analysis.

claim: Genes with RS greater than 3 had a median p-value of 0.02 in the UIH cohort.
source: They had median p-values of 0.02, 0.01, 0.11, and 0.58 in the gestational age at birth, newborn sex, birthweight, and maternal PP BMI meta-analyses, and median p-value of 0.02 in the UIH cohort.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the validation analysis.

claim: Replicating genes were enriched for processes involved in vesicle biology.
source: Replicating genes were enriched for processes involved in vesicle biology (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on data from enrichment analysis, as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Replicating genes associated with low risk were enriched for genes that are components of granulocyte specific granules (MS4A3, CEACAM8, OLR1, CAMP, LTF, CHI3L1, SLPI, PGLYRP1).
source: Specifically, replicating genes associated with low risk were enriched for genes that are components of granulocyte specific granules (MS4A3, CEACAM8, OLR1, CAMP, LTF, CHI3L1, SLPI, PGLYRP1).
evidence: The claim is based on data from enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes associated with higher risk included genes involved in vesicle sorting/production (VPS28, VTI1B, FIS1) as well as several genes involved in vesicle membrane biology (AGPAT3, ELOVL6, TM7SF2).
source: With regards to genes associated with higher risk, genes involved in vesicle sorting/production (VPS28, VTI1B, FIS1) as well as several genes involved in vesicle membrane biology (AGPAT3, ELOVL6, TM7SF2) were identified.
evidence: The claim is based on data from enrichment analysis.

claim: A significant association (R [95% confidence interval (CI)=−0.51 [–0.73, –0.18], p-value<0.01) was observed between UIH cohort Eigenvalues and number of epidemiologic risk factors.
source: Using the first Eigenvector (explaining 41.3% of variance in replicating genes), a significant association (R [95% confidence interval (CI)=−0.51 [–0.73, –0.18], p-value<0.01) was observed between UIH cohort Eigenvalues and number of epidemiologic risk factors (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is based on data from principal component analysis, as shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cord blood neutrophil abundance was inversely associated (R [95% CI]=−0.57 [–0.73, –0.34], Bonferroni p-adj<0.001) with the number of risk factors.
source: Cord blood neutrophil abundance was inversely associated (R [95% CI]=−0.57 [–0.73, –0.34], Bonferroni p-adj<0.001) with the number of risk factors (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on data from re-analysis of mass cytometry data from Olin et al., 2018, as shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Serum proteins from genes that replicated with low risk had on average negative correlations with number of risk factors.
source: Serum proteins from genes that replicated with low risk had on average negative correlations with number of risk factors (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on data from re-analysis of umbilical cord plasma-protein abundance data from Olin et al., 2018, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Proteins (CEACAM8, PGLYRP-1, CHIT1, sIL6Rα, MMP-9, and OSM) predicted to be enriched in neutrophils had strong correlations with both neutrophil abundance and number of risk factors.
source: Notably, proteins (CEACAM8, PGLYRP-1, CHIT1, sIL6Rα, MMP-9, and OSM) predicted to be enriched in neutrophils by the HPA (Uhlen et al., 2010) had strong correlations with both neutrophil abundance and number of risk factors (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is based on data from re-analysis of data from Olin et al., 2018, as shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: A significant (R [95% CI]=0.39 [0.03, 0.66], p<0.05) association was observed between PGLYRP-1 protein concentration and mRNA in the UIH cohort.
source: We observed a significant (R [95% CI]=0.39 [0.03, 0.66], p<0.05) association between PGLYRP-1 protein concentration and mRNA (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the UIH cohort, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PGLYRP-1 cord blood serum concentration was inversely associated with number of risk factors (R [95% CI]=−0.51 [–0.74, –0.17], p<0.01) in the UIH cohort.
source: Consistent with transcriptomic results, PGLYRP-1 cord blood serum concentration was inversely associated with number of risk factors (R [95% CI]=−0.51 [–0.74, –0.17], p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the UIH cohort, as shown in Figure 4D.

claim: sIL6Rα was neither associated with its mRNA in CBMCs (R [95% CI]=0.37 [–0.22, 0.77], p=0.21) nor associated with the number of risk factors (R [95% CI]=0.20 [–0.39, 0.67], p=0.50) in the UIH cohort.
source: sIL6Rα was neither associated with its mRNA in CBMCs (R [95% CI]=0.37 [–0.22, 0.77], p=0.21) nor associated with the number of risk factors (R [95% CI]=0.20 [–0.39, 0.67], p=0.50).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the UIH cohort.

claim: There was no significant difference (p>0.05, Wilcoxon rank sum test) in PGLYRP-1 or sIL6Rα between UIH and Project Viva cohorts.
source: There was no significant difference (p>0.05, Wilcoxon rank sum test) in PGLYRP-1 or sIL6Rα between UIH and Project Viva cohorts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on data comparing the UIH and Project Viva cohorts, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: PGLYRP-1 and sIL6Rα were positively correlated in both UIH (R [95% CI]=0.21 [−0.16, 0.54]) and Project Viva (R [95% CI]=0.19 [0.09, 0.29]) cohorts.
source: Consistent with our previous observations, PGLYRP-1 and sIL6Rα were positively correlated in both UIH (R [95% CI]=0.21 [−0.16, 0.54]) and Project Viva (R [95% CI]=0.19 [0.09, 0.29]) cohorts.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the UIH and Project Viva cohorts, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a negative association between PGLYRP-1 and number of risk factors in Project Viva (β [95% CI]=−0.22 [−0.36, –0.07], p-value=0.003).
source: Similar to the observation in the UIH cohort, there was a negative association between PGLYRP-1 and number of risk factors in Project Viva (β [95% CI]=−0.22 [−0.36, –0.07], p-value=0.003) (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the Project Viva cohort, as shown in Table 2.

claim: The association between PGLYRP-1 and number of risk factors in Project Viva was driven by the relationship between PGLYRP-1, gestational age, and sex.
source: This association was driven by the relationship between PGLYRP-1, gestational age, and sex.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the Project Viva cohort.

claim: There was no association of PGLYRP-1 with PP BMI or birthweight when taking into account gestational age and sex in Project Viva.
source: There was no association with PP BMI or birthweight when taking into account gestational age and sex.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the Project Viva cohort.

claim: There was no association of sIL6Rα with the number or risk factors or any individual risk factor in Project Viva.
source: Furthermore, there was no association of sIL6Rα with the number or risk factors or any individual risk factor.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the Project Viva cohort.

claim: There was an inverse relationship observed in both the UIH and Project Viva cohorts between sIL6Rα and self-reported maternal race as Black/African-American.
source: Interestingly, there was an inverse relationship observed in both the UIH and Project Viva cohorts between sIL6Rα and self-reported maternal race as Black/African-American.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the UIH and Project Viva cohorts.

claim: The abundance of PGLYRP-1 was significantly associated with current asthma at mid-childhood (adjusted odds ratio [OR] [95% CI]: 0.50 [0.31, 0.77] per 1 SD increase, p-value=0.003).
source: The abundance of PGLYRP-1 was significantly associated with current asthma at mid-childhood (adjusted odds ratio [OR] [95% CI]: 0.50 [0.31, 0.77] per 1 SD increase, p-value=0.003) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the Project Viva cohort, as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There were no significant associations between current asthma and PGLYRP-1 at the early-teen follow up.
source: There were no significant associations between current asthma and PGLYRP-1 at the early-teen follow up; however, the CI at this time point was much wider, likely secondary to the smaller sample size.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the Project Viva cohort, as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There were no significant associations between sIL6Rα with any asthma outcome at either time point.
source: There were no significant associations between sIL6Rα with any asthma outcome at either time point.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the Project Viva cohort, as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: There was no significant association between sIL6Rα and FEV1/FVCx100 ratio at either time point.
source: There was no significant association between sIL6Rα and FEV1/FVCx100 ratio at either time point.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the Project Viva cohort, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PGLYRP-1 and sIL6Rα were not associated with BDR at either time point.
source: PGLYRP-1 and sIL6Rα were not associated with BDR at either time point.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the Project Viva cohort.

claim: There was trend toward an association between PGLYRP-1 concentration and FEV1/FVCx100 ratio at mid-childhood (adjusted β [95% CI]: 1.18 [–0.18, 2.56] per 1 SD increase, p-value=0.09).
source: However, there was trend toward an association between PGLYRP-1 concentration and FEV1/FVCx100 ratio at mid-childhood (adjusted β [95% CI]: 1.18 [–0.18, 2.56] per 1 SD increase, p-value=0.09) and significant association at the early-teen follow up (adjusted β [95% CI]: 1.15 [0.20, 2.10] per 1 SD increase, p-value=0.02) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the Project Viva cohort, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was a significant association between PGLYRP-1 concentration and FEV1/FVCx100 ratio at the early-teen follow up (adjusted β [95% CI]: 1.15 [0.20, 2.10] per 1 SD increase, p-value=0.02).
source: However, there was trend toward an association between PGLYRP-1 concentration and FEV1/FVCx100 ratio at mid-childhood (adjusted β [95% CI]: 1.18 [–0.18, 2.56] per 1 SD increase, p-value=0.09) and significant association at the early-teen follow up (adjusted β [95% CI]: 1.15 [0.20, 2.10] per 1 SD increase, p-value=0.02) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the Project Viva cohort, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Assessing current asthma risk at mid-childhood, the regression model explained approximately 18% of the variance, and PGLYRP-1 was the most important predictor.
source: Assessing current asthma risk at mid-childhood, the regression model explained approximately 18% of the variance, and PGLYRP-1 was the most important predictor.
evidence: The claim is based on data from variance analysis, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Assessing current FEV1/FVCx100 at early-teen time point, the model explained approximately 26% of variance, and PGLYRP-1 was the second most important predictor.
source: Assessing current FEV1/FVCx100 at early-teen time point, the model explained approximately 26% of variance, and PGLYRP-1 was the second most important predictor (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on data from variance analysis, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Small for gestational age and children identified by their mothers as 'Other' race/ethnicity displayed significantly different associations between PGLYRP-1 and mid-childhood asthma.
source: Small for gestational age and children identified by their mothers as 'Other' race/ethnicity displayed significantly different associations between PGLYRP-1 and mid-childhood asthma.
evidence: The claim is based on data from subset analyses, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Small for gestational age and children with obese mothers displayed significantly different associations between PGLYRP-1 and FEV1/FVC.
source: Small for gestational age and children with obese mothers displayed significantly different associations between PGLYRP-1 and FEV1/FVC.
evidence: The claim is based on data from subset analyses, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lower risk individuals had higher expression of genes whose protein products are luminal (PGLRYP1, LTF, PTX3, CHI3L1, CAMP, SLPI) and membrane (CEACAM8, MS4A3, OLR1) components of specific granules.
source: In particular, lower risk individuals had higher expression of genes whose protein products are luminal (PGLRYP1, LTF, PTX3, CHI3L1, CAMP, SLPI) and membrane (CEACAM8, MS4A3, OLR1) components of specific granules (Rørvig et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on data from the study's replication analysis and is supported by a citation to Rørvig et al., 2013.

claim: The additive effect of multiple risk factors is associated with the reduction of transcription and protein products of specific granules in umbilical cord blood serum.
source: We demonstrate that the additive effect of multiple risk factors is associated with the reduction of transcription and protein products of specific granules in umbilical cord blood serum.
evidence: The claim is based on data from the study's analyses.

claim: Re-analysis of mass cytometry and proteomic data demonstrated a correlation between PGLYRP-1 in serum and neutrophil abundance.
source: Notably, our re-analysis of mass cytometry and proteomic data demonstrated a correlation between PGLYRP-1 in serum and neutrophil abundance (Olin et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on data from re-analysis of data from Olin et al., 2018.

claim: Deficiency of secretory leukocyte protease inhibitor (SLPI) leads to impairment of neutrophil development and abundance.
source: Previous literature has shown that deficiency of secretory leukocyte protease inhibitor (SLPI) leads to impairment of neutrophil development and abundance (Klimenkova et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Klimenkova et al., 2014.

claim: Individuals with specific granule deficiency syndrome have abnormal neutrophil morphology, increased susceptibility to infections, and increased risk of acute myeloid leukemia.
source: Furthermore, individuals with specific granule deficiency syndrome have abnormal neutrophil morphology, increased susceptibility to infections, and increased risk of acute myeloid leukemia (Lekstrom-Himes et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lekstrom-Himes et al., 1999.

claim: Neutrophil differentiation and survival is partially dependent on secondary granule generation.
source: Thus, this further supports the notion that neutrophil differentiation and survival is partially dependent on secondary granule generation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cited literature about SLPI deficiency and specific granule deficiency syndrome.

claim: Variation in abundance of PGLYRP-1 in serum is due to changes in neutrophil degranulation and transcription of PGLYRP1.
source: Variation in abundance of PGLYRP-1 in serum is due to changes in neutrophil degranulation and transcription of PGLYRP1, whereas sIL6Rα is derived from receptor shedding and differential splicing of its mRNAs (Jones et al., 2001; Read et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jones et al., 2001 and Read et al., 2015.

claim: sIL6Rα is derived from receptor shedding and differential splicing of its mRNAs.
